title: What the Cockroach Movement Says About the Indian Economy
gist: In a Ones and Tooze podcast excerpt, economist Adam Tooze explains that India's 'Cockroach Janta Party' protests reflect a deep structural mismatch between measured GDP growth and job creation: most new jobs are in low-productivity agriculture, formal employment sits near 23%, manufacturing has stalled at 11-13% of employment despite Apple's supply-chain buildout, and AI now threatens up to 130 million white-collar jobs — pushing India toward becoming, in Tooze's words, 'the world's biggest welfare state on a low average income.'

themes.theme: Scale and nature of India's youth jobs crisis

insights.claim: India has 367 million people between ages 15 and 29 — roughly the population of Europe just in young people — a scale that explodes conventional Western frameworks for understanding labor-market pressure.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Establishes the demographic scale that makes India's jobs crisis structurally different from anything in Western labor markets, critical context for sizing any India-focused investment or policy response.
insights.quote: There are 367 million people in India between 15 and 29. That’s most of the population of Europe, just in young people.
insights.locator: The first thing to understand is the scale

insights.claim: Modi's development strategy has produced measurable GDP growth and visible infrastructure improvement, with the top segment of Indian society reaching or exceeding developed-economy affluence, but it has not produced structural change or the job creation needed to absorb India's growing pool of graduates.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Frames India's growth as genuine but narrowly distributed — relevant to separating headline GDP optimism from the labor-market reality driving political unrest.
insights.quote: It has produced growth, but it has not produced structural change. And without structural change, it has not produced the jobs that will absorb the increasingly gigantic flow of graduates from India’s education system.
insights.locator: And so, yes, this is really a huge challenge

insights.claim: India added 83 million jobs since the pandemic — about half the size of the entire American labor force — lifting employment from 490 million to 572 million, but roughly half of those new jobs are in agriculture, where women workers are disproportionately concentrated.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Reveals that headline job-growth numbers mask a shift toward low-productivity agricultural work rather than higher-value formal employment, a key caveat for interpreting India's labor statistics.
insights.quote: India added 83 million jobs since the pandemic—that’s half the American labor force—lifting employment from 490 million to 572 million with gains for both men and women. But half of those are in farming.
insights.locator: So where most of the job growth is in India

insights.claim: The share of India's workforce in formal employment with regular contracts rose only from 18 percent in 2012 to 23 percent in 2025, meaning more than 75 percent of the population remains in informal, casualized, or precarious self-employment.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: A key structural metric showing India's formalization progress has been slow, directly relevant to labor-cost, consumer-spending-power, and social-stability assessments for India-focused investors.
insights.quote: the share of people in formal employment with regular contracts is—it rose from 18 percent in 2012 to 23 percent in 2025. Which means that 75-plus percent of the Indian population is basically in informality
insights.locator: So, this is the central problem

insights.claim: The power of insurgent mobilization in India is real because, unlike China, India is not a one-party regime with a repressive police state; Tooze frames the Cockroach Janta protests as likely 'the beginning of a rolling process of negotiation' rather than a one-off event.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Suggests continued, recurring political instability risk in India tied to jobs/education grievances, relevant to political-risk assessment for India market exposure.
insights.quote: Because this isn’t China. This isn’t a one-party regime with a repressive police state and no freedom of expression. ... But the power of insurgent mobilization in India is absolutely real.
insights.locator: So, this is the central problem that is being voiced

themes.theme: Education system: broad access, weak foundations

insights.claim: The number of accredited universities in India has exploded from 1,600 in 1991 to 70,000 today, with the biggest jumps occurring in the 2000s, reflecting a genuine widening of access to higher education.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of India's higher-education expansion, relevant to assessing the addressable talent pool for outsourcing, IT services, and knowledge-economy investment in India.
insights.quote: the number of universities has exploded from 1,600 accredited institutions in 1991 to 70,000 today, with huge jumps especially in the 2000s.
insights.locator: And over the last 30 to 40 years

insights.claim: India's top university, the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, ranks only 118th in global university rankings, compared with China which increasingly dominates the global top 10.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: A stark India-China comparison in elite higher-education quality that bears on each country's capacity to produce globally competitive research and innovation talent.
insights.quote: India’s top university, the Indian Institute of Technology in Delhi, at least by the conventional university rankings, ranks at 118th in the global rankings—by comparison with China, which increasingly dominates the top 10.
insights.locator: And on the other hand, there is

insights.claim: The deepest concern raised by Tooze's contacts in India is elementary education, where outcomes are poor due to underpaid teachers who often don't show up and low household cultural capital, particularly among mothers from older, often illiterate generations.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Identifies the root-cause bottleneck (elementary education quality, not university access) constraining India's long-term human-capital formation — a factor for long-horizon India growth forecasts.
insights.quote: The teachers are underpaid, the teachers don’t show up. And crucially, of course, there’s very little cultural capital in the households, and particularly with mothers, many of whom are from older generations who are illiterate
insights.locator: So in India, really, again, there’s huge change

insights.claim: India's Right to Education Act of 2009 established that schools must exist in every village and that children must attend, producing near-comprehensive school enrollment over the past 20 years, but comprehensive enrollment has not translated into comparable learning outcomes.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Distinguishes access (largely achieved) from quality (still lacking) in India's education system, a nuance important for calibrating expectations of India's future skilled-labor pipeline.
insights.quote: The Right to Education Act of 2009 has now firmly established that there must be schools in every village, that there is a requirement that kids attend school.
insights.locator: So in India, really, again, there’s huge change

insights.claim: When the World Bank first engaged with post-Maoist China in the early 1980s, it discovered near-comprehensive literacy despite using India as its benchmark for what a poor country looked like — highlighting a decades-old gap in basic human-capital formation between the two countries.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Provides historical context for why China outpaced India in industrialization and manufacturing competitiveness — a foundational literacy gap dating back over 40 years.
insights.quote: their standard of what a poor country looked like was India, and then they discovered post-Maoist China, which actually had near-comprehensive literacy, and they hadn’t seen anything like it.
insights.locator: And this was evident already in the early 1980s

themes.theme: AI threat and the stalled manufacturing pivot

insights.claim: According to some of the more alarmist surveys, AI is a potentially lethal threat to roughly 130 million Indian jobs, threatening virtually the entire routine white-collar sector — a devastating risk for an economy that never fully industrialized via manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: A specific, large-scale jobs-at-risk estimate for AI displacement in India's IT/services-heavy economy, directly relevant to sizing AI's macro labor-market impact in emerging markets.
insights.quote: according to some of the more alarmist surveys—in India it’s something like 130 million jobs, virtually the entire routine white-collar sector is potentially at risk, which would be devastating for an economy which has not principally gone down the manufacturing route.
insights.locator: AI is potentially a lethal threat

insights.claim: Only 11 to 13 percent of Indian employment is in manufacturing — the level typically seen in a highly developed, post-industrial economy — despite India never having gone through a full industrialization phase, raising the central question of why India hasn't replicated Bangladesh's or Vietnam's low-cost manufacturing success.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: A striking anomaly — India's manufacturing employment share resembles a developed economy despite lacking the corresponding development, implying blocked industrial-policy channels worth investigating for manufacturing-relocation investment theses.
insights.quote: between 11 percent and 13 percent of Indian employment is in manufacturing, which is the sort of level you’d expect in a highly developed economy having gone through industrialization and come out the other side.
insights.locator: The manufacturing story is the central question

insights.claim: Obstacles cited for India's weak low-wage manufacturing base include the historical License Raj regulatory regime, high wages and job security in the public sector that crowd out private industrial employment, in addition to China's undervalued exchange rate used for its own industrial policy.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Identifies specific structural and policy barriers to Indian manufacturing competitiveness that would need to be addressed for India to capture supply-chain diversification away from China.
insights.quote: Including the License Raj, the notoriously dense network of regulation, the incredibly high wages and security that are offered to public servants, which create a kind of crowding-out effect.
insights.locator: And then they flip to a more introspective mode

insights.claim: Apple has established substantial smartphone production lines in India by importing significant capital and Chinese technical talent, defying skeptics including Tooze himself who doubted a China-based supply chain could be replicated there — but this success has not spawned a broader manufacturing transformation, as illustrated by India's garment production remaining smaller than Bangladesh's.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Direct evidence that even a high-profile manufacturing success story (Apple) has not triggered spillover industrialization in India — a cautionary signal for investors betting on broad 'China plus one' manufacturing gains in India.
insights.quote: by importing a lot of money and an awful lot of Chinese technical talent, they have actually set up now substantial smartphone production lines in India. But it hasn’t spawned a dramatic transformation of a larger scale.
insights.locator: And again, it’s important to see past the headlines

insights.claim: Facing stalled manufacturing, saturated tech job creation, and a low-productivity agricultural sector, Tooze says the emerging consensus in Delhi is that India's future may be to become the world's biggest welfare state on a low average income — a role explicitly written into the Indian constitution's social-democratic provisions.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: A striking long-run framing for India's economic trajectory — investors modeling India's consumption and fiscal path should weigh the likelihood of expanding welfare transfers rather than a manufacturing-led income convergence.
insights.quote: Does that mean that our future is the world’s biggest welfare state on a low average income? And the answer seems to be yes.
insights.locator: This is exactly the train of thought

insights.claim: Over the winter of 2025-26, the Modi government mounted a concerted attack on India's rural jobs-guarantee program (promising up to 100 days of public-works employment per family per year), massively scaling it back after years of it being an iconic and contested pillar of the Indian welfare state.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Documents a major, recent policy rollback of India's flagship rural employment guarantee, a concrete data point for assessing rural income and consumption risk in India.
insights.quote: over the winter of ’25, ’26, the Modi government mounted a concerted attack on this program, massively scaling it back.
insights.locator: Modi’s people hated it

insights.claim: In place of the jobs-guarantee program, the Modi government has substituted charismatic, consumption-based deliverables — public toilets, subsidized clean cooking gas, and expanded free or cheap grain access established in law — alongside a highly effective digital direct-transfer system enabling governments to send money instantly to citizens' phones.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Describes a shift in India's welfare-delivery model from employment guarantees to targeted consumption subsidies and digital cash transfers, relevant to consumer-spending forecasts and fintech/digital-payments investment themes in India.
insights.quote: practically everyone is equipped with some form of smartphone or some form of cellphone. And once you’re in the system, it’s literally a digital money technology... regional governments in India, national governments can ping money to the population directly.
insights.locator: And then on the other hand, this other element

insights.claim: Tooze describes India's digital direct-transfer infrastructure as more advanced than comparable Western systems, contrasting it favorably with the slow paper-check processes in the U.S. and Germany's inability to operate a population-wide digital benefits system.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Highlights an underappreciated Indian fintech/digital-infrastructure advantage relative to developed economies — a potential positive differentiator for India's digital-payments and govtech sector.
insights.quote: It’s not the ridiculous printing presses of checks that the Americans have to go through, or like the German administration, which can’t even operate a digital system for the whole population. It’s truly a remarkably innovative system.
insights.locator: There’s literally a direct channel

insights.claim: India is currently running live policy experiments comparing 'drip-drip-drip' monthly basic-income-style welfare payments against lump-sum allocations designed to let households buy capital equipment or pay off debt, which Tooze calls an underrated global laboratory in low-income welfare design.
insights.speaker: Adam Tooze
insights.so_what: Flags India as a live testbed for welfare-transfer design that could inform policy in other emerging markets, relevant to development-economics and social-policy investment theses.
insights.quote: there’s a series of experiments going on about whether or not the most effective mechanism is a kind of drip, drip, drip welfare provision... or if you’re better off doing lump-sum allocations... It’s really a laboratory of experimentation in low-income welfare.
insights.locator: And so then there’s a series of experiments

themes.theme: Origins of the Cockroach Janta Party protests

insights.claim: The Cockroach Janta Party movement emerged after India's chief justice referred to the country's unemployed youth as 'cockroaches' earlier in 2026, sparking parliament marches met with police crackdowns and internet shutdowns, ultimately forcing the government to back down and the education minister to resign.
insights.speaker: Cameron Abadi
insights.so_what: Establishes the proximate political trigger and near-term outcome (a ministerial resignation) of the protest movement, useful as a marker of political risk materializing from youth unemployment grievances.
insights.quote: When India’s chief justice referred to unemployed youth in India as cockroaches earlier this year, that became the rallying cry for a new political movement called the Cockroach Janta Party.
